title: Receptor Timing: Add Up the Waits
endLine: Steps set when: slowest on and off steps set onset and duration.

scenes.tts: A muscle channel opens almost at once; a heart receptor waits on a G protein. Now watch estradiol, a fat-soluble hormone, slip through the membrane with no relay. Why can that route still take hours?
scenes.caption: A muscle channel opens almost at once; a heart receptor waits on a G protein. Now watch estradiol, a fat-soluble hormone, slip through the membrane with no relay. Why can that route still take hours?
scenes.visual: Continue the cell cross-section from the first film in 16:9 on a dark background. A horizontal GREY plasma membrane spans the upper third above cytosol, with a faint GREY nuclear curve at lower right and a shared bottom timeline marked 'schematic'. On the left, GOLD acetylcholine binds a CYAN five-block muscle channel and a CYAN trace spikes at '< 1 ms'. In the centre, GOLD acetylcholine binds a TEAL seven-bar receptor that activates a PURPLE G protein and a BLUE potassium channel, with a BLUE trace rising at 'tens of ms'. On the right, an AMBER estradiol token slips smoothly through the GREY membrane directly to a CORAL nuclear receptor with no relay block, yet the timeline stretches to 'hours?' beside a bright question mark. Keep at most six elements active; no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: A muscle channel opens almost at once; a heart receptor waits on a G protein. Now watch estradiol, a fat-soluble hormone, slip through the membrane with no relay. Why can that route still take hours?

scenes.visual: Over the carried three-route cell cross-section, show the title 'Receptor Timing: Add Up the Waits' for two seconds. GOLD acetylcholine and AMBER estradiol tokens drift gently, and the bottom timeline markers ('< 1 ms', 'tens of ms', 'hours?') pulse softly.

scenes.tts: Each step from binding to output must finish before the next starts. Onset time is roughly the sum of those waits. A muscle channel needs only binding and opening. Each takes tens of microseconds, finishing well under a millisecond.
scenes.caption: Each step from binding to output must finish before the next starts. Onset time is roughly the sum of those waits. A muscle channel needs only binding and opening. Each takes tens of microseconds, finishing well under a millisecond.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto the left CYAN muscle channel in the same GREY membrane while the other routes dim. Show two end-to-end wait blocks assembling along the bottom timeline marked 'schematic': first a GOLD block labelled '1. binding' as two GOLD acetylcholine tokens dock on the CYAN pore, then a CYAN block labelled '2. pore opening' as the pore widens and CYAN ions flow through. A bracket under both reads 'tens of µs each' and snaps to '< 1 ms'. At most five objects on screen; no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Each step from binding to output must finish before the next starts. Onset time is roughly the sum of those waits. A muscle channel needs only binding and opening. Each takes tens of microseconds, finishing well under a millisecond.

scenes.tts: The heart route has four steps, and exchange, swapping G D P for G T P, is the slowest. Alone, a G protein releases G D P zero point four four times a minute. One over zero point four four is a mean wait of about two point three minutes.
scenes.caption: The heart route has four steps, and exchange, swapping GDP for GTP, is the slowest. Alone, a G protein releases GDP 0.44 times a minute. 1 ÷ 0.44 is a mean wait of about 2.3 minutes.
scenes.visual: Slide along the same GREY membrane to centre the TEAL seven-bar muscarinic receptor, PURPLE G protein holding a RED 'GDP' tag, and BLUE potassium channel. Build four wait segments along the schematic timeline as each moves: brief '1. binding' (GOLD token docks on TEAL), long '2. GDP exchange' (RED tag clings to PURPLE while a timer climbs to '1 ÷ 0.44 ≈ 2.3 min' unaided, written as it is spoken, then shrinks sharply when TEAL engages and swaps RED 'GDP' for GREEN 'GTP'), brief '3. G protein shift' (PURPLE parts separate or rearrange), and '4. channel opens' (BLUE pore opens). Keep segment 2 visibly the longest bar.
scenes.narration: The heart route has four steps, and exchange, swapping GDP for GTP, is the slowest. Alone, a G protein releases GDP 0.44 times a minute. 1 ÷ 0.44 is a mean wait of about 2.3 minutes.

scenes.tts: Suppose the occupied receptor speeds release a thousandfold. Zero point four four times a thousand is four hundred forty a minute, about seven point three a second. One over seven point three gives a mean wait near one hundred forty milliseconds. But a cell holds many G proteins. Must it wait that long for current?
scenes.caption: Suppose the occupied receptor speeds release 1,000-fold. 0.44 × 1,000 is 440 a minute, about 7.3 a second. 1 ÷ 7.3 gives a mean wait near 140 ms. But a cell holds many G proteins. Must it wait that long for current?
scenes.visual: Keep the heart membrane in view and pull slightly back so a row of many PURPLE G proteins holding RED 'GDP' sits beneath GOLD-bound TEAL receptors. Write '0.44 × 1,000 = 440/min ≈ 7.3/s' then '1 ÷ 7.3 ≈ 140 ms' as each is spoken. Place a live clock bar along the bottom with '0 ms' at left and a bright marker at '140 ms (mean)'. Show a BLUE current trace panel at lower right masked behind a question mark. Across the top, show 'Must the cell wait 140 ms?' in bright TEXT. Do not flip any G proteins to GREEN or reveal the curve yet.
scenes.narration: Suppose the occupied receptor speeds release 1,000-fold. 0.44 × 1,000 is 440 a minute, about 7.3 a second. 1 ÷ 7.3 gives a mean wait near 140 ms. But a cell holds many G proteins. Must it wait that long for current?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the question 'Must the cell wait 140 ms?', the '140 ms (mean)' marker, and the masked BLUE current panel. GOLD-bound TEAL receptors pulse gently above the row of PURPLE G proteins while the clock cursor hovers near '0 ms'. Do not reveal the onset time or answer.

scenes.tts: No. The fraction on by time t is one minus e to the minus seven point three t. That reaches ten percent at about fourteen milliseconds, and current can start. Channels need several G protein pieces, a little extra delay. So steps set when: waits add up, and the slowest sets the pace.
scenes.caption: No. The fraction on by time t is 1 − e^(−7.3t). That reaches 10% at about 14 ms, and current can start. Channels need several G protein pieces, a little extra delay. So steps set when: waits add up, and the slowest sets the pace.
scenes.visual: Replace the question with 'No: early fraction starts current'. Start the clock from '0 ms': individual PURPLE G proteins flip randomly to GREEN 'GTP' as a computed curve f(t) = 1 - exp(-7.3*t) draws from 0 to 400 ms (computed from 440/min, ~7.3/s). Show the formula '1 − e^(−7.3t)' as it is spoken, then highlight '10% on at ~14 ms' well left of 'mean wait ~140 ms'. On the beta-gamma line, cluster several small PURPLE subunits (schematic count) onto the BLUE channel to show a brief lag before the BLUE trace climbs. Fade the curve into the shared bottom wait bar with a bright banner: 'Steps set when'.
scenes.narration: No. The fraction on by time t is 1 − e^(−7.3t). That reaches 10% at about 14 ms, and current can start. Channels need several G protein pieces, a little extra delay. So steps set when: waits add up, and the slowest sets the pace.

scenes.tts: Now slower designs. Single-pass kinase receptors cross the membrane once and carry a phosphate-attaching enzyme. A ligand pairs chains, or rearranges a pair, so the enzymes tag each other and recruit partners. Those steps take seconds to minutes.
scenes.caption: Now slower designs. Single-pass kinase receptors cross the membrane once and carry a phosphate-attaching enzyme. A ligand pairs chains, or rearranges a pair, so the enzymes tag each other and recruit partners. Those steps take seconds to minutes.
scenes.visual: Pan along the same GREY membrane to show two ORANGE single-pass stems crossing the membrane once, each with an inner enzyme block. A GOLD ligand brings the two stems together (and briefly animates an alternative pre-paired rearrangement beneath the label 'pair or rearrange'). Inside, the ORANGE blocks touch, add bright GOLD phosphate dots to each other, and draw in a WHITE partner block. On the shared bottom timeline marked 'schematic', an ORANGE wait bar stretches across 'seconds to minutes'. At most five objects; no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Now slower designs. Single-pass kinase receptors cross the membrane once and carry a phosphate-attaching enzyme. A ligand pairs chains, or rearranges a pair, so the enzymes tag each other and recruit partners. Those steps take seconds to minutes.

scenes.tts: Now the puzzle. Estradiol slips inside and binds its nuclear receptor, skipping every relay. But its output is new R N A within minutes, then new protein over tens of minutes to hours. One slow step outweighs every skipped relay.
scenes.caption: Now the puzzle. Estradiol slips inside and binds its nuclear receptor, skipping every relay. But its output is new RNA within minutes, then new protein over tens of minutes to hours. One slow step outweighs every skipped relay.
scenes.visual: Move down into the same cell toward the GREY nuclear envelope arc. An AMBER estradiol token glides straight through the GREY membrane into the cell and snaps into a CORAL nuclear receptor, which grips a WHITE DNA bar directly with an empty gap where relays would sit labelled 'no relay'. From the DNA bar, WHITE strips labelled 'new RNA' emerge at 'minutes', then build into CORAL blocks labelled 'new protein' as the schematic timeline extends to 'tens of min to hours'. Compare that single long CORAL bar beside the short CYAN channel bar.
scenes.narration: Now the puzzle. Estradiol slips inside and binds its nuclear receptor, skipping every relay. But its output is new RNA within minutes, then new protein over tens of minutes to hours. One slow step outweighs every skipped relay.

scenes.tts: Duration follows the same rule: signals last until their slowest off step finishes. Muscle current decays in about a millisecond once acetylcholine clears. G proteins stay on for seconds until they split G T P. New proteins can keep a gene program running after the hormone leaves.
scenes.caption: Duration follows the same rule: signals last until their slowest off step finishes. Muscle current decays in about a millisecond once acetylcholine clears. G proteins stay on for seconds until they split GTP. New proteins can keep a gene program running after the hormone leaves.
scenes.visual: Pull back to show the carried cell with three stacked schematic off-bars along the bottom timeline after ligand disappears above the GREY membrane. Top row (CYAN): GOLD acetylcholine vanishes and the CYAN pore snaps shut, decaying in '~1 ms'. Middle row (PURPLE/BLUE): TEAL receptor empties, yet PURPLE G proteins remain GREEN 'GTP' until each flips back to RED 'GDP', holding the BLUE channel open for 'seconds'. Bottom row (CORAL): AMBER estradiol leaves, yet CORAL 'new protein' blocks stay active, labelled 'outlasts the hormone'. Label the bracket 'slowest off step'.
scenes.narration: Duration follows the same rule: signals last until their slowest off step finishes. Muscle current decays in about a millisecond once acetylcholine clears. G proteins stay on for seconds until they split GTP. New proteins can keep a gene program running after the hormone leaves.

scenes.tts: This rule has limits. High enzymatic gain can buy back speed, because multiplied output crosses a threshold sooner. Potency, how much ligand a route needs, is separate from speed. And estradiol has reported rapid surface actions.
scenes.caption: This rule has limits. High enzymatic gain can buy back speed, because multiplied output crosses a threshold sooner. Potency, how much ligand a route needs, is separate from speed. And estradiol has reported rapid surface actions.
scenes.visual: Keep the carried membrane world and display three concise limit panels in sequence beside the schematic timeline. First, one TEAL receptor fans arrows into many GREEN enzyme blocks labelled 'high gain' while a schematic output trace rises steeply and crosses a dashed 'threshold' line sooner than a low-gain trace. Second, show two separate dials labelled 'potency' and 'speed' moving independently. Third, show an AMBER estradiol token touching a small '?' marker on the outer GREY membrane labelled 'reported rapid surface actions' without replacing the slow nuclear route below.
scenes.narration: This rule has limits. High enzymatic gain can buy back speed, because multiplied output crosses a threshold sooner. Potency, how much ligand a route needs, is separate from speed. And estradiol has reported rapid surface actions.

scenes.tts: Design does more than count steps. The slowest waits, on and off, set when a signal starts and how long it lasts.
scenes.caption: Design does more than count steps. The slowest waits, on and off, set when a signal starts and how long it lasts.
scenes.visual: Return to the wide carried cell view showing the CYAN channel, TEAL GPCR with PURPLE G protein, ORANGE single-pass pair, and CORAL nuclear receptor above the shared schematic timeline. Under each route, its on-bar and off-bar glow in turn, the longest of each brightest, labelled 'slowest on' and 'slowest off'. Keep all four routes gently breathing. Answer no Predict question from the lesson.
scenes.narration: Design does more than count steps. The slowest waits, on and off, set when a signal starts and how long it lasts.

scenes.visual: End card with one line only: 'Steps set when: slowest on and off steps set onset and duration.' Set it large and centred on the dark background. No title, logo, URL, subtitle or smaller line appears. Behind the text, muted CYAN, PURPLE, ORANGE and CORAL wait bars drift subtly along a faint timeline.
